extracted.intended_audience: working mathematicians (authors of research and expository papers), including early-career researchers and graduate students
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on preparing, choosing a venue for, submitting, responding to referees for, and publishing mathematical research and expository articles, plus advice on collaboration and professional society membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference placement strategy (in-text vs end-of-chapter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice between end-of-chapter bibliography and in-text, on-the-fly references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End-of-chapter approach “serves the big shots well” but may overlook smaller contributors. In-text referencing “systematically holds you accountable”: you state a theorem or recall an idea and give the reference immediately, making you less likely to give someone short shrift. The final choice is up to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek feedback before submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicit colleague feedback via conversations, seminars, and circulating preprints to gauge reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have told colleagues, given seminars, or sent preprints, you should have a sense of whether listeners are surprised, impressed, confused, or bored. Consider criticisms and suggestions carefully and make appropriate changes to your paper before choosing where to submit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding when work is worth writing up
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate when partial results, failed attempts, or evolving problems deserve exposition as papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful mathematicians can take partial results and failures and turn them into an attractive tapestry of theorems, corollaries, partial results and conjectures. Avoid dumping years of work in the trash; manage your research program so it proceeds incrementally and yields reportable progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-submission rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit a paper to only one journal at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never send the same paper to two different journals simultaneously: you risk being caught if the same referee sees both submissions. Wait for a decision from journal n before submitting to journal (n+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a journal by subject fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit to journals that publish cognate results and whose editors/referees will understand your paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by considering where similar results have appeared (e.g., Journal of Algebra for algebra topics). Consider which editors will understand your paper and select suitable referees; you need not know the editor personally but it's useful to know their perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a journal by prestige/backlog/turnaround tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance desire for a high-rank journal with potential long refereeing times, backlogs, and higher rejection likelihood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting to top journals may mean slow refereeing, long backlog, or rejection for various reasons. If facing tenure/clock issues, consider shooting lower to optimize for quicker acceptance. Form an opinion by seeing what papers appear in journals, who is on editorial boards, and by consulting experienced colleagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available data on journals (backlog/turnaround)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate a journal's backlog and typical turnaround time before submitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices of the AMS publishes analyses with this information. Consider these statistics when choosing where to submit, especially if timing matters for career milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow 'Instructions to Authors'
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and follow a journal's submission instructions regarding formatting, copies, keywords, languages, and electronic submission preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions tell you how many copies are needed, whether title/abstract should be separate, AMS classifications, language acceptance, formatting, TeX style files, and whether electronic submissions are accepted. Not following these causes delays and annoys editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic submission practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When submitting via journal web forms, fill required fields and upload the requested files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Web submission systems prompt for necessary information and are reliable; you typically send a PDF initially. The journal will often assume the submitter is the communicating author unless told otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicating (corresponding) author convention
rubrics_metrics.description: The person who submits the paper is usually assumed to be the communicating author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All further correspondence will be with that person and that email address unless you explicitly tell the journal otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letter tone and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the cover letter to the editor simple and dispassionate; avoid over-promotional pitches and naming potential referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fulsome praise is usually unhelpful and may annoy editors. Naming potential referees may rule them out if perceived as personal friends; a short factual cover letter is best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use manuscript number in correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference the journal-assigned manuscript number in future communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A manuscript number prevents misfiling as the paper moves between staff, editors, and referees. Use it consistently when querying the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and handle wait times; when to follow up
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical wait for a referee report is 4–6 months; after that, a polite inquiry is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After waiting several months, send a polite note stating submission and acknowledgement dates and ask for progress; most editors will nudge the appropriate associate editor or referee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret referee reports pragmatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee reports vary from brief endorsements to multi-page critiques; be objective and use the feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports may say 'terrific' or 'dreadful' or something between. A rejection doesn't necessarily mean the paper is bad (backlog, wrong referee, misunderstandings). Perseverance is key; learn from reports and resubmit elsewhere if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to referee comments in revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Address referee remarks item-by-item and document what you did in a cover letter when resubmitting a revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the editor conditions acceptance on detailed responses, you are expected to reply to each of the referee's remarks. You can state where a referee is mistaken or respectfully disagree on taste, but address each point. This is the best way to continue business with the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledging helpful referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider thanking the referee in the paper's acknowledgements if the referee was particularly helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to identify the referee by name; a generic acknowledgment is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make TeX source self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing the TeX source (usually submitted after acceptance), ensure all macros and font calls are included so the file compiles elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on in-house macros/fonts from your university's system. Initially you may submit only a PDF, but upon acceptance journals will request the source; make it portable so the journal can compile it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofing galley/page proofs meticulously
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully proofread proofs for mathematical and typesetting accuracy and respond to author queries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return proofs quickly (often within 48 hours). You may need to sign approval for the version going to print. Respond to each author query and annotate PDFs if required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic early publication and archival copy note
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals publish accepted papers electronically before print; the archival copy is typically the hard copy after copy-editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the online immediate version may lack final copy editing; the printed version is the archival record in many fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reprints are largely obsolete
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals commonly provide a PDF of the final article rather than paper reprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can print any reprints they need from the PDF; journals may still ask how many reprints you want but this is often an atavism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set collaboration ground rules at the outset
rubrics_metrics.description: Agree on priorities, division of labor, and authorship conventions before starting a collaborative project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agreement to collaborate is an a priori contract to see things through. Do not leave priority or authorship questions until the project is finished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and courtesy in collaborations
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain mutual respect; avoid deceptive or adversarial behavior among collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful long-term collaborations accept that contributions will vary across projects. Avoid introducing errors deliberately, unilateral withdrawal/resubmission, or disputes over minor naming/numbering details. Alphabetical authorship is 'almost always best.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate about follow-on work building on joint results
rubrics_metrics.description: If new work builds on prior joint work, inform former collaborators and discuss authorship appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: call the collaborator, propose joint authorship if appropriate, or offer to acknowledge earlier contributions. Courteous early contact usually avoids disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Join and engage with professional societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership in societies (e.g., AMS, MAA, SIAM) yields career and community benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Societies organize conferences, publish journals and book series, produce Math Reviews/MathSciNet, lobby for mathematics, sponsor prizes/fellowships, and support infrastructure. Even small societies can be touchstones for members; young mathematicians should join.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository writing: target audience and balance of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: For expository/survey articles, reach a broader audience by balancing explanation versus technical detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume readers are experts in the specific jargon; do not prove central theorems in full but describe ingredients and give rough sketches. Anticipate audience shortcomings and adjust presentation (more like teaching, but without live feedback).

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert talks to surveys appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-hour invited talk can be turned into a survey article, but adapt content for readers rather than listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys aim at broader readership; provide background, motivation, and clear exposition rather than full technical proofs. Be mindful of goals and audience when preparing expository pieces.
